module_title: Banking and Financial Awareness: Negotiable Instruments and Cheques (Level 2: Intermediate)
introduction: This intermediate level delves into the 'Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881', differentiating between Promissory Notes and Bills of Exchange. We will also explore the rules of 'Crossing' of cheques, which are staple questions in PO and Clerk Mains exams.

core_concepts.title: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
core_concepts.description:
Negotiable instruments in India are governed by the NI Act 1881. From an exam perspective, the 3 most crucial sections are:
- Section 4: Promissory Note
- Section 5: Bill of Exchange
- Section 6: Cheque

core_concepts.title: Promissory Note vs. Bill of Exchange
core_concepts.description:
- Promissory Note: Written by the Debtor (borrower). It contains an 'unconditional promise' to pay. It involves only 2 parties: the Maker and the Payee.
- Bill of Exchange: Written by the Creditor (lender). It contains an 'unconditional order' to pay. It involves 3 parties: Drawer, Drawee, and Payee.

core_concepts.title: Crossing of a Cheque (Section 123)
core_concepts.description: Drawing two parallel transverse lines on the top-left corner of a cheque is called 'Crossing'. Its main purpose is safety. A crossed cheque cannot be encashed at the bank counter; the money must be credited directly into the bank account of the payee (Account Payee).

important_entities.name: The Currency Note Exception
important_entities.key_fact: Bank notes issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) do NOT fall under the definition of a Promissory Note.
important_entities.significance: Even though a currency note says "I promise to pay the bearer the sum of...", the RBI Act 1934 explicitly excludes currency notes from being classified as a 'Promissory Note' under the NI Act 1881.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A frequent exam question: 'Why can a cheque bounce, but a DD cannot?' The reason is that a cheque is issued by an individual, whereas a Demand Draft is issued by the 'Bank' itself after already collecting the funds from you. Therefore, a DD can never be dishonored due to insufficient funds.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Memorize them in alphabetical order starting from P: P for Promissory Note (4), B for Bill of Exchange (5), and C for Cheque (6). This instantly solves 'Match the Following' questions.

exam_strategy_tips: In PO exams, they ask the difference between 'General Crossing' and 'Special Crossing'. In Special Crossing, the name of a specific bank (e.g., SBI) is written between the two parallel lines, meaning the cheque can only be credited to an account held in that specific bank.
